prompt: A wiki page says that nothing runs as root. What does moving that rule into the repository as code add?

choices.text: It runs on every push
choices.why: Right, and it refuses before merge: the rule no longer depends on somebody remembering it at review.

choices.text: It makes the containers run as a non-root user
choices.why: The rule refuses a file that breaks it; the Dockerfile or manifest is what sets the user.

choices.text: New developers read it in their first week
choices.why: That is what the wiki page already got, and it is the weak part.

choices.text: Nobody needs to review it any more
choices.why: A rule as code is reviewed more, in every commit that changes it.

prompt: Match each name to what it is.

pairs.right: an engine that evaluates rules over a JSON document
the language the rules are written in
a command that parses configuration files and runs the rules over them
OPA running as a Kubernetes admission controller

right_distractors: a registry that stores signed images

prompt: Which candidate rule passes the lesson's test for being worth writing as code?

choices.text: Code is reviewed by somebody who understands it
choices.why: No file shows understanding, so no parser can check it.

choices.text: Every container declares a memory limit
choices.why: Right. A manifest shows it, the answer is yes or no, and a container without one can starve its node.

choices.text: Memory limits are sensible for the workload
choices.why: Sensible needs a person or an indefensible number; it is not yes or no.

choices.text: YAML files are indented with spaces, never tabs
choices.why: A file shows it, but nobody is hurt; it would teach people to ignore the stage.

prompt: policy/docker.rego has three deny rules. How does conftest combine them?

choices.text: All three must fail for the file to fail
choices.why: One message in the set is enough to fail the file.

choices.text: Only the first rule that fires is reported
choices.why: Every rule that holds adds its message; the run printed all of them.

choices.text: One set, deny; any message fails
choices.why: Right. Each rule that holds adds its message; separate rules are alternatives joined into one set.

choices.text: They are evaluated in order and stop at the first false line
choices.why: Lines inside one rule must all hold, but separate rules do not stop each other.

prompt: linkbox's image runs as 65532, yet the user rule failed on lesson 15's Dockerfile. Why?

choices.text: The distroless image runs as root by default
choices.why: It runs as 65532; docker image inspect printed it.

choices.text: The Dockerfile never states the user
choices.why: Right. The user came from the base image, and a check that reads the file sees only what the file says.

choices.text: The rule reads the wrong stage
choices.why: It reads the final stage, which is the one that ships; there was no USER in it.

choices.text: conftest cannot parse multi-stage Dockerfiles
choices.why: It parsed both stages and numbered them 0 and 1.

prompt: A colleague proposes USER nonroot instead of USER 65532:65532, since the name is clearer. What goes wrong with the manifests of lesson 10?

choices.text: The image would run as root
choices.why: nonroot is a real user in the distroless image; the image would not run as root.

choices.text: The registry would refuse the image
choices.why: The registry stores whatever is pushed; the user is not its concern.

choices.text: Nothing; a name and a number are equivalent
choices.why: They are equivalent inside the image, and not to the kubelet checking runAsNonRoot.

choices.text: runAsNonRoot cannot be checked against a name
choices.why: Right: the kubelet refuses to start the pod. It needs a number to know the user is not 0, which is why the rule asks for one.

prompt: When a Rego helper such as final_user has no value, it is ___, and not final_user is then true.
conftest ran the 7 rules of policy/kubernetes.rego against the documents in k8s/. How many tests did it report?
Why does the policy read the tag from the part of the image name after the last slash?

choices.text: Because a digest uses a slash
choices.why: A digest follows @, which the rule checks separately.

choices.text: localhost:5000 has a colon of its own
choices.why: Right, so the whole name always looks tagged. Checking the whole string for a colon would pass localhost:5000/linkbox, which has no tag.

choices.text: Because Kubernetes ignores the registry part
choices.why: Kubernetes pulls from the registry the name gives; it does not ignore it.

choices.text: Because tags are case-sensitive
choices.why: Case has nothing to do with where the tag starts.

prompt: Somebody changes the admission binding's validationActions from Deny to Audit. What would a cluster show, without the policy stage?

choices.text: kubectl apply fails, because Audit is not a valid value
choices.why: Audit is a valid action; the binding installs.

choices.text: Every Deployment is refused until the binding is fixed
choices.why: Audit does the opposite: nothing is refused.

choices.text: A warning on every kubectl command
choices.why: Audit records; it does not warn the client. Warn would.

choices.text: Nothing different; every Deployment gets through
choices.why: Right, and the policy is still listed. That silence is why the pipeline checks the policy's own settings.

prompt: The hurried edit changed the image to linkbox:latest and readOnlyRootFilesystem to false. Which rules failed? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: the read-only root filesystem
choices.why: Right. One of the two edited lines.

choices.text: the floating tag
choices.why: Right. linkbox:latest ends in :latest.

choices.text: the registry
choices.why: Right. linkbox:latest does not start with localhost:5000/.

choices.text: the memory limit
choices.why: The limit was not touched, and the run reported three failures, not four.

choices.text: runAsNonRoot
choices.why: The pod still sets runAsNonRoot: true.

prompt: After the floating rule was "simplified" to check the whole name for a colon, conftest test on k8s/ still passed 35 of 35. Why?

choices.text: linkbox's image has a tag
choices.why: Right, and the broken line only matters without one. The real manifests never exercise the case; only a test does.

choices.text: conftest caches results between runs
choices.why: It evaluates the rules afresh every time.

choices.text: The change made the rule stricter, not weaker
choices.why: It made it weaker: localhost:5000/linkbox now passes untagged.

choices.text: conftest test does not read policy changes until committed
choices.why: It reads the files on disk, committed or not.

prompt: Why does each test assert one exact message rather than only that deny is not empty?

choices.text: Rego cannot count the elements of a set at all
choices.why: count() works on sets; the good-input tests use it.

choices.text: conftest verify requires a message
choices.why: verify only needs the test's body to hold.

choices.text: To catch a rule that fires for the wrong reason
choices.why: Right. A different rule's message would make "not empty" pass.

choices.text: Messages are faster to compare than sets
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the tests run in well under a second either way.

prompt: You add a rule that refuses a Deployment with hostNetwork: true. Which test is the one most worth writing first?

choices.text: One that runs the rule against the real k8s/ files
choices.why: Those files pass today; a test against them proves nothing about the rule firing.

choices.text: One where hostNetwork: true gives its message
choices.why: Right, its exact message. It shows the deny fires at least once, which a passing manifest never shows.

choices.text: One that times the rule on a large manifest
choices.why: Speed is not where a policy fails; silence is.

choices.text: One where hostNetwork is absent and deny is empty
choices.why: Useful later, but it passes even if the rule never fires.

prompt: Trivy flags linkbox's manifest with KSV-0125, images from an untrusted registry. What is the right reading?

choices.text: Move the image to Docker Hub, where Trivy trusts it
choices.why: That would break this project's own rule and lesson 10's admission policy.

choices.text: The check is wrong for this project
choices.why: Right: its only trusted registry is localhost:5000. A library cannot know your registry; your own rule does.

choices.text: The registry needs TLS before anyone trusts it
choices.why: The finding is about which registry, not how it is reached.

choices.text: Delete the image tag and let the cluster pick one
choices.why: A missing tag would break a different rule and fix nothing here.

prompt: Why does the pipeline gate on conftest and not on trivy config?

choices.text: trivy config is slower
choices.why: Speed is not among the reasons given; both are quick on three files.

choices.text: trivy config cannot read Kubernetes manifests
choices.why: It read them and raised four findings.

choices.text: Its checks change under you, and some contradict decisions
choices.why: Right: the bundle updates itself. A gate should fail on reviewed decisions, not on a library's opinions.

choices.text: Trivy checks are not written in Rego
choices.why: They are written in Rego, the same language as yours.

prompt: Trivy raises KSV-0020 because the manifest sets no runAsUser above 10000, although the image runs as 65532. What does that share with DS-0002 on lesson 15's Dockerfile?

choices.text: Both are false positives to put in .trivyignore
choices.why: Both are fair: each file leaves out a fact it could state.

choices.text: Both come from the same Rego rule
choices.why: One is a Dockerfile check and one a Kubernetes check.

choices.text: Both mean the container runs as root
choices.why: It runs as 65532 in both cases.

choices.text: Each file leaves the fact to the image
choices.why: Right. Stating it in the file, USER or runAsUser, answers both.

prompt: Put the first stages of ci/stages, as this lesson leaves it, in the order they run.
ci/policy.sh runs conftest verify before conftest test. What would go wrong the other way round?

choices.text: conftest test would refuse to run without verified rules
choices.why: It runs any rules it is given; that is the danger.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as both run
choices.why: With set -e, a failing test stage stops first and the order decides what the log says.

choices.text: Passes from a broken rule would be trusted
choices.why: Right. Verify first, so no pass is trusted from a rule that no longer refuses.

choices.text: verify would test the files instead of the rules
choices.why: verify runs the test_ rules; it never reads the project's files.

prompt: The same registry rule is enforced in the pipeline and at admission. Which situation does only admission stop?

choices.text: A pull request that changes k8s/linkbox.yaml to another registry
choices.why: The pipeline refuses that commit before it is ever applied.

choices.text: A rule test that no longer fires
choices.why: That is conftest verify, in the pipeline.

choices.text: A Dockerfile whose base image has no digest
choices.why: That is a pipeline check; admission never sees a Dockerfile.

choices.text: kubectl apply from a laptop
choices.why: Right, with a manifest that never went through the repository. Only the cluster sees objects that did not come from a commit.

prompt: A new rule needs to check that every Service in k8s/ has type ClusterIP. Where does it go, and what proves it works?

choices.text: In ci/stages as a new stage, proved by the next push
choices.why: A push of manifests that pass shows nothing about the rule firing.

choices.text: In policy/kubernetes.rego, with a test in kubernetes_test.rego that expects its message
choices.why: Right. Same package, same stage, and a test that sees it fire.

choices.text: In policy/docker.rego, which already runs in the pipeline
choices.why: That package runs on the Dockerfile only, with --namespace docker.

choices.text: In k8s/admission.yaml only, so the cluster refuses it
choices.why: That leaves the author to find out at deploy time; the lesson argues for both doors.

prompt: A team copies this lesson's policies into another service whose images are built FROM scratch with a static binary. Which rule will fail at once, and is that right?

choices.text: The memory-limit rule; it is wrong for static binaries
choices.why: Memory limits are about the container, not how its binary was linked.

choices.text: The registry rule; it is fine
choices.why: The registry rule reads manifests, not FROM lines.

choices.text: The digest rule; scratch needs an exception
choices.why: Right: scratch has no digest, because it is not an image to pin, and a test should cover the exception.

choices.text: None; every rule here applies to any image
choices.why: Rules encode one project's decisions, and FROM scratch breaks the digest rule's assumption.
